text.tspan: What Explains Variation in State Compliance
with the Laws of Armed Conflict Under
This paper explains variation in compliance with the Laws of Armed Conflict (LOAC) under
asymmetric conditions where reciprocity is weak or absent. Using the 1991 Gulf War, the
2006 Israel-Hezbollah War, and the Russo-Ukrainian War as comparative cases, it argues
that international reputation acts as a substitute compliance mechanism when material
reciprocity fails. Actors dependent on external legitimacy, diplomatic backing, or military
assistance maintain greater restraint toward civilians, while actors insulated from audience
costs are more likely to use LOAC violations instrumentally for tactical advantage.
The paper also identifies a boundary condition: reputational incentives can weaken when
perceived security costs of restraint exceed expected political penalties.

g.text: Keywords: Laws of Armed Conflict, International Humanitarian Law, compliance in war,
reciprocity, reputation, asymmetric warfare, civilian protection
